claim: ORMDL3 gene polymorphisms are genetically associated with bronchial asthma.
source: Mounting evidence has demonstrated the genetic association of ORMDL sphingolipid biosynthesis regulator 3 (ORMDL3) gene polymorphisms with bronchial asthma and a diverse set of inflammatory disorders.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by references to existing literature on ORMDL3 polymorphisms and asthma.

claim: ORMDL3 gene polymorphisms are genetically associated with inflammatory disorders.
source: Mounting evidence has demonstrated the genetic association of ORMDL sphingolipid biosynthesis regulator 3 (ORMDL3) gene polymorphisms with bronchial asthma and a diverse set of inflammatory disorders.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by references to existing literature.

claim: ORMDL3 is a negative modulator of type I IFN signaling.
source: Herein, we report that ORMDL3 is a negative modulator of the type I IFN signaling by interacting with mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) and subsequently promoting the proteasome-mediated degradation of retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing ORMDL3's effects on IFN signaling.

claim: ORMDL3 interacts with MAVS.
source: Herein, we report that ORMDL3 is a negative modulator of the type I IFN signaling by interacting with mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) and subsequently promoting the proteasome-mediated degradation of retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: ORMDL3 promotes proteasome-mediated degradation of RIG-I.
source: Herein, we report that ORMDL3 is a negative modulator of the type I IFN signaling by interacting with mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) and subsequently promoting the proteasome-mediated degradation of retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing RIG-I degradation upon ORMDL3 overexpression and rescue by proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: ORMDL3 binds to USP10.
source: Immunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry (IP-MS) assays uncovered that ORMDL3 binds to ubiquitin-specific protease 10 (USP10), which forms a complex with and stabilizes RIG-I through decreasing its K48-linked ubiquitination.
evidence: This claim is supported by IP-MS data and co-IP validation experiments.

claim: USP10 forms a complex with RIG-I.
source: Immunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry (IP-MS) assays uncovered that ORMDL3 binds to ubiquitin-specific protease 10 (USP10), which forms a complex with and stabilizes RIG-I through decreasing its K48-linked ubiquitination.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP experiments showing interaction between USP10 and RIG-I.

claim: USP10 stabilizes RIG-I through decreasing its K48-linked ubiquitination.
source: Immunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry (IP-MS) assays uncovered that ORMDL3 binds to ubiquitin-specific protease 10 (USP10), which forms a complex with and stabilizes RIG-I through decreasing its K48-linked ubiquitination.
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assays showing decreased K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I upon USP10 overexpression.

claim: ORMDL3 disrupts the interaction between USP10 and RIG-I.
source: ORMDL3 thus disrupts the interaction between USP10 and RIG-I, thereby promoting RIG-I degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP experiments showing reduced USP10-RIG-I interaction in the presence of ORMDL3.

claim: Inhibition of ORMDL3 enhances anti-tumor efficacy in subcutaneous syngeneic tumor models in C57BL/6 mice.
source: Additionally, subcutaneous syngeneic tumor models in C57BL/6 mice revealed that inhibition of ORMDL3 enhances anti-tumor efficacy by augmenting the proportion of cytotoxic CD8 positive T cells and IFN production in the tumor microenvironment (TME).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth experiments showing reduced tumor growth upon ORMDL3 knockdown.

claim: Inhibition of ORMDL3 augments the proportion of cytotoxic CD8 positive T cells in the tumor microenvironment.
source: Additionally, subcutaneous syngeneic tumor models in C57BL/6 mice revealed that inhibition of ORMDL3 enhances anti-tumor efficacy by augmenting the proportion of cytotoxic CD8 positive T cells and IFN production in the tumor microenvironment (TME).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased activated CD8+ T cells in ORMDL3 knockdown tumors.

claim: Inhibition of ORMDL3 augments IFN production in the tumor microenvironment.
source: Additionally, subcutaneous syngeneic tumor models in C57BL/6 mice revealed that inhibition of ORMDL3 enhances anti-tumor efficacy by augmenting the proportion of cytotoxic CD8 positive T cells and IFN production in the tumor microenvironment (TME).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased expression of ISGs in ORMDL3 knockdown tumors.

claim: Type I IFN play a key role in the innate immune response to viral infections.
source: Type I interferon (type I IFN) play a key role in the innate immune response to viral infections.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Under viral stimulations, cells produce and release interferons, which induce the transcription of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs).
source: Under viral stimulations, cells produce and release interferons, which induce the transcription of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) (Dalskov et al., 2023; McNab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Type I IFN produced by malignant tumor cells or infiltrating immune cells influence the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy.
source: Besides their critical role in antiviral immune responses, growing evidence suggests that type I IFN produced by malignant tumor cells or infiltrating immune cells also influence the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy (Zitvogel et al., 2015; Holicek et al., 2024; Gajewski et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: Many traditional chemotherapeutic drugs require intact type I IFN signaling to fully exert their effects.
source: Many traditional chemotherapeutic drugs, targeted anti-tumor drugs, immunoadjuvants, and oncolytic viruses require intact type I IFN signaling to fully exert their effects (Yang et al., 2014; Zitvogel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: High intratumoral expression levels of type I IFN or ISGs are associated with positive disease outcomes in cancer patients.
source: Furthermore, studies have shown that high intratumoral expression levels of type I IFN or ISGs are associated with positive disease outcomes in cancer patients (Spaapen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: In response to viral RNA molecules, RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs) exposed their caspase activation and recruitment domains (CARD) and then cooperate with MAVS and TBK1 to promote the production of type I IFN.
source: In response to viral RNA molecules, RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs) exposed their caspase activation and recruitment domains (CARD) and then cooperate with mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) and TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) to promote the production of type I IFN (Rehwinkel and Gack, 2020).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TBK1 phosphorylates and activates IRF3 and IRF7, which then induce the expression of type I IFN and various ISGs.
source: TBK1 phosphorylates and activates IRF3 and IRF7, which then induce the expression of type I IFN and various ISGs (Goubau et al., 2013; Hartmann, 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Targeting RLRs can provoke anti-infection activities.
source: Thus, targeting RLRs can provoke anti-infection activities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of RLRs in antiviral immunity.

claim: RLRs play an important role in anti-tumor immunity.
source: Moreover, RLRs also play an important role in anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent examples and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting RLRs sensitizes 'immune cold' tumors to become 'immune hot' tumors.
source: For example, targeting RLRs sensitizes 'immune cold' tumors to become 'immune hot' tumors (Cheon et al., 2014).

claim: DNA methyltransferase inhibitors upregulate endogenous retroviruses in tumor cells to induce the activation of the RLR-mediated RNA recognition pathway that potentiates immune checkpoint therapy.

claim: SB9200 is an orally available prodrug of a dinucleotide agonist of RIG-I and NOD2.

claim: ORMDL3 significantly inhibited poly(I:C)-stimulated transcription of IFNB1.
source: The result showed that ORMDL3 significantly inhibited poly(I:C) and VSV stimulated transcription of IFNB1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ORMDL3 significantly inhibited VSV-stimulated transcription of IFNB1.
source: The result showed that ORMDL3 significantly inhibited poly(I:C) and VSV stimulated transcription of IFNB1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ORMDL3 overexpression resulted in a marked reduction in the phosphorylation level of IRF3.
source: Western blots demonstrated a marked reduction in the phosphorylation level of IRF3 when ORMDL3 was overexpressed (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ectopic expression of ORMDL3 in A549 cells attenuated IFNB1 expression induced by poly(I:C) but not poly(dG:dC).
source: Ectopic expression of ORMDL3 in A549 cells attenuated IFNB1 expression induced by poly(I:C) but not poly(dG:dC) (Figure 1C).

claim: In mouse bone marrow-derived primary macrophages (BMDM), ORMDL3 attenuated IFNB1 expression induced by poly(I:C) but not poly(dG:dC).
source: This phenomenon was also observed in parallel experiments using mouse bone marrow-derived primary macrophages (BMDM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ORMDL3 is a repressor of RNA-induced type I IFN expression.
source: These findings highlight ORMDL3 as a repressor of RNA-induced type I IFN expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing ORMDL3's selective inhibition of RNA-induced IFN expression.

claim: ORMDL3 decreases the IFNβ luciferase reporter activity induced by RIG-I.
source: ORMDL3 was found to decrease the IFNβ luciferase reporter activity induced by RIG-I while showing no effect on cGAS/STING or TRIF (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ORMDL3 shows no effect on cGAS/STING-induced IFNβ luciferase reporter activity.
source: ORMDL3 was found to decrease the IFNβ luciferase reporter activity induced by RIG-I while showing no effect on cGAS/STING or TRIF (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ORMDL3 shows no effect on TRIF-induced IFNβ luciferase reporter activity.
source: ORMDL3 was found to decrease the IFNβ luciferase reporter activity induced by RIG-I while showing no effect on cGAS/STING or TRIF (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ORMDL3 knockdown strikingly suppressed the replication of VSV.
source: We found that ORMDL3 knockdown strikingly suppressed the replication of VSV, whereas overexpression of ORMDL3 enhanced the replication of VSV (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral replication assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Overexpression of ORMDL3 enhanced the replication of VSV.
source: We found that ORMDL3 knockdown strikingly suppressed the replication of VSV, whereas overexpression of ORMDL3 enhanced the replication of VSV (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral replication assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ORMDL3 knockdown showed no significant difference in HSV-1 viral replication.
source: We also infected shNC and shORMDL3 A549 stable cell lines with herpes simplex virus-1 (HSV-1) and found no significant difference in viral replication (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral replication assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: ORMDL3 only facilitates RNA virus replication but not DNA virus.
source: These results suggest that ORMDL3 only facilitates RNA virus replication but not DNA virus, which coincides with the finding that ORMDL3 specifically represses RNA- but not DNA-induced type I IFN expression (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of ORMDL3 on RNA vs DNA virus replication and IFN induction.

claim: ORMDL3 inhibited IFNB1 mRNA expression induced by RIG-I.
source: Further quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) results indicated that ectopic expression of ORMDL3 inhibited IFNB1 mRNA expression and transcription of downstream genes CCL5 and CXCL10 induced by RIG-I and MAVS but not TBK1 or IRF3-5D (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ORMDL3 inhibited CCL5 transcription induced by RIG-I.
source: Further quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) results indicated that ectopic expression of ORMDL3 inhibited IFNB1 mRNA expression and transcription of downstream genes CCL5 and CXCL10 induced by RIG-I and MAVS but not TBK1 or IRF3-5D (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ORMDL3 inhibited CXCL10 transcription induced by RIG-I.
source: Further quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) results indicated that ectopic expression of ORMDL3 inhibited IFNB1 mRNA expression and transcription of downstream genes CCL5 and CXCL10 induced by RIG-I and MAVS but not TBK1 or IRF3-5D (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ORMDL3 inhibited IFNB1 mRNA expression induced by MAVS.
source: Further quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) results indicated that ectopic expression of ORMDL3 inhibited IFNB1 mRNA expression and transcription of downstream genes CCL5 and CXCL10 induced by RIG-I and MAVS but not TBK1 or IRF3-5D (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ORMDL3 did not inhibit IFNB1 mRNA expression induced by TBK1.
source: Further quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) results indicated that ectopic expression of ORMDL3 inhibited IFNB1 mRNA expression and transcription of downstream genes CCL5 and CXCL10 induced by RIG-I and MAVS but not TBK1 or IRF3-5D (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: MDA5-induced IFN upregulation was inhibited by ORMDL3.
source: Additionally, MDA5-induced IFN upregulation was also inhibited by ORMDL3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ORMDL3 knockdown significantly increased the expression of IFNB1, CCL5, and ISG54 induced by RIG-I-N.
source: Since ORMDL3 was downregulated in response to VSV stimulation in HEK293T, we first transfected cells with siORMDL3 followed by secondary transfection with RIG-I-N (an active form of RIG-I, 1–200aa of RIG-I) in HEK293T, and we found that ORMDL3 knockdown significantly increased the expression of IFNB1, CCL5, and ISG54 (Figure 2C) as well as the protein abundance of RIG-I (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ORMDL3 knockdown increased the protein abundance of RIG-I.
source: Since ORMDL3 was downregulated in response to VSV stimulation in HEK293T, we first transfected cells with siORMDL3 followed by secondary transfection with RIG-I-N (an active form of RIG-I, 1–200aa of RIG-I) in HEK293T, and we found that ORMDL3 knockdown significantly increased the expression of IFNB1, CCL5, and ISG54 (Figure 2C) as well as the protein abundance of RIG-I (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a negative correlation between ORMDL3 levels and RIG-I protein expression.
source: Subsequent experiments involving various signaling proteins such as RIG-I (WT/RIG-I-N), MDA5, TBK1, and IRF3 indicated a negative correlation between ORMDL3 levels and RIG-I/RIG-I-N protein expression, with maximal degradation observed in RIG-I-N (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Maximal degradation by ORMDL3 was observed in RIG-I-N.
source: Subsequent experiments involving various signaling proteins such as RIG-I (WT/RIG-I-N), MDA5, TBK1, and IRF3 indicated a negative correlation between ORMDL3 levels and RIG-I/RIG-I-N protein expression, with maximal degradation observed in RIG-I-N (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Only ORMDL3 can facilitate the degradation of RIG-I-N among ORMDL family members.
source: To investigate whether ORMDL3 is unique in promoting RIG-I degradation, we compared ORMDL1, 2, and 3. When we co-expressed RIG-I-N with them, we found that only ORMDL3 can facilitate the degradation of RIG-I-N (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Human RIG-I can be degraded upon ORMDL3 overexpression.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that human RIG-I and murine Rig-I can be degraded upon ORMDL3/Ormdl3 overexpression, implying that ORMDL3's function is conservative in humans and mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Murine Rig-I can be degraded upon Ormdl3 overexpression.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that human RIG-I and murine Rig-I can be degraded upon ORMDL3/Ormdl3 overexpression, implying that ORMDL3's function is conservative in humans and mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: ORMDL3's function is conservative in humans and mice.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that human RIG-I and murine Rig-I can be degraded upon ORMDL3/Ormdl3 overexpression, implying that ORMDL3's function is conservative in humans and mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both human and murine RIG-I are degraded by ORMDL3.

claim: ORMDL3 overexpression eliminated endogenous RIG-I protein abundance.
source: In addition, ORMDL3 overexpression also eliminated endogenous RIG-I protein abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: ORMDL3 only decreased the protein abundance of RIG-I-N but not RIG-I-C.
source: We ectopically expressed an increasing amount of Flag-ORMDL3 with the RIG-I-N and the RIG-I-C truncated form (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) and found that ORMDL3 only decreased the protein abundance of RIG-I-N (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: RIG-I was degraded upon the stimulation of poly(I:C) in the presence of ORMDL3.
source: We co-transfected ORMDL3 and RIG-I with or without poly(I:C) and found that RIG-I was degraded upon the stimulation of poly(I:C), suggesting that ORMDL3 degrades RIG-I only when it was activated and the CARD was exposed (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ORMDL3 degrades RIG-I only when it was activated and the CARD was exposed.
source: We co-transfected ORMDL3 and RIG-I with or without poly(I:C) and found that RIG-I was degraded upon the stimulation of poly(I:C), suggesting that ORMDL3 degrades RIG-I only when it was activated and the CARD was exposed (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RIG-I degradation by ORMDL3 requires poly(I:C) stimulation.

claim: Co-expression of ORMDL3 suppressed RIG-I-N-induced expression of IFNB1 and CCL5.
source: Further examination showed that co-expression of ORMDL3 suppressed RIG-I-N-induced expression of IFNB1 and CCL5, as well as pro-inflammatory cytokines IL6 and TNF (Figure 2H), suggesting its role on both NF-κB and type I IFN pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Co-expression of ORMDL3 suppressed RIG-I-N-induced expression of IL6 and TNF.
source: Further examination showed that co-expression of ORMDL3 suppressed RIG-I-N-induced expression of IFNB1 and CCL5, as well as pro-inflammatory cytokines IL6 and TNF (Figure 2H), suggesting its role on both NF-κB and type I IFN pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The degradation of RIG-I-N mediated by ORMDL3 could be blocked by MG132 but not CQ.
source: We co-expressed ORMDL3 and RIG-I-N and treated cells with proteasome inhibitor MG132, and lysosome inhibitor CQ. We found the degradation of RIG-I-N mediated by ORMDL3 could be blocked by MG132 but not CQ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ORMDL3 promotes K48-linked ubiquitination on RIG-I-N.
source: To investigate the mechanism, we co-transfected RIG-I-N, ORMDL3, and plasmids encoding different forms of ubiquitin. The results indicated an increase in K48-linked ubiquitination on RIG-I-N, implicating ORMDL3 in promoting proteasomal degradation of RIG-I (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The degradation-promoting effect of ORMDL3 on RIG-I-N-KR was nullified.
source: To pinpoint the lysine residues crucial for RIG-I ubiquitination, we engineered a mutant version of RIG-I-N in which all lysines were mutated to arginines, denoted as RIG-I-N-KR. Intriguingly, the degradation-promoting effect of ORMDL3 on RIG-I-N-KR was nullified (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RIG-I-N mutant1 was resistant to degradation by ORMDL3.
source: Remarkably, the results showed that mutant1 was resistant to degradation by ORMDL3 (Figure 3D), suggesting that the last nine lysines on RIG-I-N may mediate its degradation induced by ORMDL3.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The last nine lysines on RIG-I-N may mediate its degradation induced by ORMDL3.
source: Remarkably, the results showed that mutant1 was resistant to degradation by ORMDL3 (Figure 3D), suggesting that the last nine lysines on RIG-I-N may mediate its degradation induced by ORMDL3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutant1 (with last nine lysines mutated) is resistant to ORMDL3-mediated degradation.

claim: Individual mutations K146R, K154R, K164R, and K172R did not impede ORMDL3-induced RIG-I degradation.
source: To delve deeper into the intricate mechanism of ORMDL3-induced degradation of RIG-I, we initially introduced single-point mutations, specifically K146R, K154R, K164R, and K172R (Rehwinkel and Gack, 2020), which have been reported important for the function and stability of RIG-I. Co-transfection with ORMDL3 revealed that these individual mutations did not impede the degradation process, hinting at the potential cooperation of lysine residues (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The RIG-I-N-4KR mutant displayed resistance to degradation by ORMDL3.
source: We then mutated all four lysine residues and assessed ORMDL3-induced RIG-I-N degradation. Strikingly, the RIG-I-N-4KR mutant, in which K146, K154, K164, and K172 were simultaneously mutated to arginines, displayed resistance to degradation by ORMDL3 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The RIG-I-N 4KR mutant failed to exhibit the upregulation of K48-linked ubiquitination induced by ORMDL3 overexpression.
source: At the meantime, the RIG-I-N 4KR mutant failed to exhibit the upregulation of K48-linked ubiquitination induced by ORMDL3 overexpression, reinforcing the pivotal role played by K146, K154, K164, and K172 in mediating RIG-I ubiquitination and subsequent degradation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: K146, K154, K164, and K172 play a pivotal role in mediating RIG-I ubiquitination and subsequent degradation.
source: At the meantime, the RIG-I-N 4KR mutant failed to exhibit the upregulation of K48-linked ubiquitination induced by ORMDL3 overexpression, reinforcing the pivotal role played by K146, K154, K164, and K172 in mediating RIG-I ubiquitination and subsequent degradation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutation of these four lysines prevents ORMDL3-mediated ubiquitination and degradation.

claim: When Ormdl3 was overexpressed in BMDM, endogenous Rig-I was downregulated.
source: In addition, we found that when Ormdl3 was overexpressed in BMDM, endogenous Rig-I was downregulated (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Only Flag-tagged MAVS interacted with ORMDL3-GFP among tested proteins.
source: Next, we sought to determine the binding partner of ORMDL3 in the type I IFN pathway. Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) and immunoblot analysis showed that only Flag-tagged MAVS interacted with ORMDL3-GFP (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of the transmembrane domain (TM) of MAVS abrogated the interaction with ORMDL3.
source: To delineate the requisite domains of MAVS facilitating this interaction, various MAVS truncations were co-transfected with ORMDL3. Notably, deletion of the transmembrane domain (TM) of MAVS abrogated the interaction, while deletion of the CARD had no discernible impact (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of the CARD of MAVS had no discernible impact on the interaction with ORMDL3.
source: To delineate the requisite domains of MAVS facilitating this interaction, various MAVS truncations were co-transfected with ORMDL3. Notably, deletion of the transmembrane domain (TM) of MAVS abrogated the interaction, while deletion of the CARD had no discernible impact (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All four ORMDL3 truncations (1–42aa, 43–82aa, 83–118aa, and 119–153aa) interact with MAVS.
source: To map the essential domains of ORMDL3 that mediate its association with MAVS, we generated four truncations of ORMDL3 based on the structure, which are 1–42aa, 43–82aa, 83–118aa, and 119–153aa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, upper panel). Intriguingly, we found that all these four ORMDL3 truncations interact with MAVS (Figure 4C) and impede RIG-I-N-induced transcription of IFNB1, CCL5, ISG54, and ISG56 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All four ORMDL3 truncations impede RIG-I-N-induced transcription of IFNB1, CCL5, ISG54, and ISG56.
source: To map the essential domains of ORMDL3 that mediate its association with MAVS, we generated four truncations of ORMDL3 based on the structure, which are 1–42aa, 43–82aa, 83–118aa, and 119–153aa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, upper panel). Intriguingly, we found that all these four ORMDL3 truncations interact with MAVS (Figure 4C) and impede RIG-I-N-induced transcription of IFNB1, CCL5, ISG54, and ISG56 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Each domain of ORMDL3 is favorable to RIG-I-N degradation.
source: In addition, co-transfection of RIG-I-N-Myc with individual ORMDL3 truncations showed that each domain of ORMDL3 is favorable to RIG-I-N degradation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both N- and C-terminal truncations of ORMDL3 retained the ability to interact with MAVS.
source: Moreover, inspired by Guo et al.'s discovery of a naturally occurring short isoform of ORMDL3 (Jin et al., 2011), we engineered N- and C-terminal truncations of ORMDL3 to mimic this isoform (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, lower panel), and the results showed that both truncations of ORMDL3 retained the ability to interact with MAVS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FRET experiment showed a direct interaction between ORMDL3 and MAVS with FRET efficiency of 24.40519%.
source: To further validate the association between ORMDL3 and MAVS, we performed a FRET experiment in HeLa cells. In this experiment, we co-overexpressed YFP-MAVS (donor) and CFP-ORMDL3 (acceptor). When we bleached YFP-MAVS, we noticed that the fluorescence of CFP-ORMDL3 increased, indicating a direct interaction between ORMDL3 and MAVS (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: IP-MS analysis identified USP10 as a potential candidate that interacts with ORMDL3.
source: To identify the E3 ligase or deubiquitinase involved in ORMDL3-mediated RIG-I ubiquitination, we conducted immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) analysis using Flag-ORMDL3 as bait and identified USP10 as a potential candidate (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by IP-MS data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-IP experiment demonstrated the interaction between ORMDL3 and USP10.
source: We validated the IP-MS results and the co-IP experiment revealed that only USP10 can interact with ORMDL3 but not CAND1 or UFL1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Subsequent co-IP validation demonstrated the interaction between ORMDL3 and USP10, USP10 and RIG-I, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Co-IP experiment demonstrated the interaction between USP10 and RIG-I.
source: We validated the IP-MS results and the co-IP experiment revealed that only USP10 can interact with ORMDL3 but not CAND1 or UFL1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Subsequent co-IP validation demonstrated the interaction between ORMDL3 and USP10, USP10 and RIG-I, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The RIG-I level is decreased in USP10 stable knockdown HEK293T cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that the RIG-I level is decreased in USP10 stable knockdown HEK293T cells while overexpression of USP10 promotes the accumulation of RIG-I (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Overexpression of USP10 promotes the accumulation of RIG-I.
source: Interestingly, we found that the RIG-I level is decreased in USP10 stable knockdown HEK293T cells while overexpression of USP10 promotes the accumulation of RIG-I (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: USP10 overexpression decreased K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I.
source: As USP10 is a deubiquitinase, we investigated its impact on RIG-I ubiquitination and observed a decrease in K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I upon USP10 overexpression (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: USP10 failed to increase the RIG-I-N-4KR level.
source: Co-transfection USP10 with RIG-I-N or its 4KR mutant showed that USP10 failed to increase the RIG-I-N-4KR level, underscoring the indispensability of these four lysine residues (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: ORMDL3's ability to degrade RIG-I-N was markedly compromised in USP10 knockdown cells.
source: Upon overexpressing RIG-I-N and ORMDL3 in USP10 knockdown cells, ORMDL3's ability to degrade RIG-I-N was markedly compromised, emphasizing the indispensable role of USP10 in this degradation process (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: ORMDL3 disrupts the interaction between RIG-I and USP10.
source: Co-IP experiments unveiled robust binding of USP10 to both RIG-I and ORMDL3, and ORMDL3 disrupts the interaction between RIG-I and USP10 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: USP10 exhibited a specific role in stabilizing RIG-I, but not other innate immune proteins such as MAVS, MDA5, and IRF3.
source: Crucially, USP10 exhibited a specific role in stabilizing RIG-I, but not other innate immune proteins such as MAVS, MDA5, and IRF3, and this effect can be reversed by ORMDL3 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The function of ORMDL3 in disturbing USP10-mediated RIG-I stabilization could be rescued by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 but not the lysosome inhibitor CQ.
source: Further investigations showed that the function of ORMDL3 in disturbing USP10-mediated RIG-I stabilization could be rescued by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 but not the lysosome inhibitor CQ (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RIG-I-N-KR or RIG-I-N-mutant1 was necessary to prevent USP10-induced accumulation and ORMDL3-mediated degradation.
source: Subsequent co-transfection experiments delineated that RIG-I-N-KR or RIG-I-N-mutant1 was necessary to prevent USP10-induced accumulation and ORMDL3-mediated degradation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Single-point mutation of the K146, K154, K164, or K172 residue on RIG-I-N does not affect the regulation of USP10 and ORMDL3.
source: Notably, single-point mutation of the K146, K154, K164, or K172 residue on RIG-I-N does not affect the regulation of USP10 and ORMDL3 (Figure 6E), whereas the RIG-I-N-4KR mutation abolished this process (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The RIG-I-N-4KR mutation abolished the regulation by USP10 and ORMDL3.
source: Notably, single-point mutation of the K146, K154, K164, or K172 residue on RIG-I-N does not affect the regulation of USP10 and ORMDL3 (Figure 6E), whereas the RIG-I-N-4KR mutation abolished this process (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: USP10 decreased K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I-N.
source: Building upon these observations, we sought to elucidate whether USP10 influences RIG-I ubiquitination through these four sites. Co-expression of HA-K48Ub and RIG-I-N-GFP with or without USP10 revealed a decrease in K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I-N by USP10 and this effect was nullified in the presence of the 4KR mutant, which is in consistent with ORMDL3-mediated regulation (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The effect of USP10 on K48-linked ubiquitination was nullified in the presence of the 4KR mutant.
source: Building upon these observations, we sought to elucidate whether USP10 influences RIG-I ubiquitination through these four sites. Co-expression of HA-K48Ub and RIG-I-N-GFP with or without USP10 revealed a decrease in K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I-N by USP10 and this effect was nullified in the presence of the 4KR mutant, which is in consistent with ORMDL3-mediated regulation (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: USP10 expression increased mRNA levels of IFNB1, CCL5, and ISG54.
source: Additionally, we verified the functional consequences of USP10-induced RIG-I stabilization by assessing the mRNA levels of IFNB1, CCL5, and ISG54, which were increased upon enforced USP10 expression and reduced upon co-expression with ORMDL3 (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Co-expression of ORMDL3 with USP10 reduced mRNA levels of IFNB1, CCL5, and ISG54.
source: Additionally, we verified the functional consequences of USP10-induced RIG-I stabilization by assessing the mRNA levels of IFNB1, CCL5, and ISG54, which were increased upon enforced USP10 expression and reduced upon co-expression with ORMDL3 (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The deficiency of ORMDL3 significantly suppressed LCC tumor growth compared to the control group.
source: To assess the impact of ORMDL3 on anti-tumor activity, we conducted knockdown experiments targeting ORMDL3 in LLC and MC38 murine cancer cell lines, followed by subcutaneous inoculation into C57BL/6 mice. The deficiency of ORMDL3 significantly suppressed LCC tumor growth compared to the control group (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: Tumor growth inhibition by targeting ORMDL3 was validated in the MC38 cancer model.
source: This tumor growth inhibition by targeting ORMDL3 was further validated in the MC38 cancer model (Figure 7G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7G–I.

claim: In both LLC and MC38 knockdown cell lines, the protein level of Rig-I was significantly upregulated.
source: Moreover, in both LLC and MC38 knockdown cell lines, the protein level of Rig-I was significantly upregulated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D), and its upregulation was further verified by western blots in LLC tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) in MC38 tumors (Figure 7K).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and IHC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–E and Figure 7K.

claim: In the LLC tumor model, the knockdown of ORMDL3 led to a significant increase in the expression of ISGs, including Ccl5, Cxcl10, Tnf, and Il6.
source: Moreover, investigations revealed that in the LLC tumor model, the knockdown of ORMDL3 led to a significant increase in the expression of ISGs, including Ccl5, Cxcl10, Tnf, and Il6, compared to the control group (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In the MC38 cancer model, ORMDL3 knockdown resulted in significantly elevated Ifnb1, Ccl5, and Cxcl10 mRNA levels.
source: This upregulation of ISGs upon ORMDL3 knockdown was consistent in the MC38 cancer model, where Ifnb1, Ccl5, and Cxcl10 mRNA levels were significantly elevated (Figure 7J).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated an increase in CD3+ T cell infiltration percentage in LLC tumors when ORMDL3 was knocked down.
source: Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated an increase in CD3+ T cell infiltration percentage in LLC tumors when ORMDL3 was knocked down (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Activated CD8+ T cells (CD8+ CD107a+ and CD8+ CD44+) exhibited an increase in the ORMDL3 knockdown group.
source: Notably, although CD8+ cell levels showed no significant change among groups (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), activated CD8+ T cells (CD8+ CD107a+ and CD8+ CD44+) exhibited an increase in the ORMDL3 knockdown group (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claim: IHC assays revealed that more CD8+ T cells were infiltrated in ORMDL3 knockdown MC38 tumors.
source: In addition, IHC assays revealed that more CD8+ T cells were infiltrated in ORMDL3 knockdown MC38 tumors (Figure 7K).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: Inhibition of tumor-intrinsic ORMDL3 amplifies anti-tumor immunity by increasing ISGs expression in TME and promoting cytotoxic CD8+ T cell activation.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that inhibition of tumor-intrinsic ORMDL3 amplifies anti-tumor immunity by increasing ISGs expression in TME and promoting cytotoxic CD8+ T cell activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined observations of increased ISGs and activated CD8+ T cells in ORMDL3 knockdown tumors.

claim: Higher expression of ORMDL3 was observed in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), colon adenocarcinoma, and lung squamous cell carcinoma compared to their corresponding normal samples.
source: We further analyzed ORMDL3 expression in the TCGA-pan-cancers cohort. We observed higher expression of ORMDL3 in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), colon adenocarcinoma, and lung squamous cell carcinoma compared to their corresponding normal samples (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In LUAD cohorts, high ORMDL3 expression was associated with poor prognosis, as indicated by overall survival, progression-free survival, and disease-specific survival analyses.
source: In LUAD cohorts, high ORMDL3 expression was associated with poor prognosis, as indicated by overall survival, progression-free survival, and disease-specific survival analyses (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Analysis of LUAD cohorts revealed enrichment of stromal scores in tumors with low ORMDL3 expression.
source: Analysis of LUAD cohorts also revealed enrichment of stromal scores in tumors with low ORMDL3 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: A negative correlation was found between ORMDL3 expression and the ESTIMATE score.
source: Additionally, we found a negative correlation between ORMDL3 expression and the ESTIMATE score, indicating a potential association between ORMDL3 expression and immune cell infiltration (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: ORMDL3 expression showed a negative correlation with CD8+ T cell activation markers such as PRF1, GZMA, and GZMB.
source: Interestingly, ORMDL3 expression showed a negative correlation with CD8+ T cell activation markers such as PRF1, GZMA, and GZMB, as well as with ISGs such as CCL5 and CXCL10 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F), validating our finding that ORMDL3 serves as a negative regulator of the IFN signaling pathway and anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2F.

claim: ORMDL3 expression showed a negative correlation with ISGs such as CCL5 and CXCL10.
source: Interestingly, ORMDL3 expression showed a negative correlation with CD8+ T cell activation markers such as PRF1, GZMA, and GZMB, as well as with ISGs such as CCL5 and CXCL10 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F), validating our finding that ORMDL3 serves as a negative regulator of the IFN signaling pathway and anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The RIG-I MAVS pathway is essential for the early detection of viral infections and the initiation of an effective antiviral immune response.
source: The RIG-I MAVS pathway is essential for the early detection of viral infections and the initiation of an effective antiviral immune response.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: The RIG-I MAVS pathway has two major downstream signaling events: the interferon signaling and the pro-inflammatory cytokine signal axis.
source: This pathway has two major downstream signaling events: the interferon signaling and the pro-inflammatory cytokine signal axis (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: During RNA virus infection, MAVS recruits TBK1, which phosphorylates IRF3 and IRF7, leading to the production of type I IFN.
source: During RNA virus infection, MAVS recruits TBK1, which phosphorylates IRF3 and IRF7, leading to the production of type I IFN.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: The pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling pathway primarily operates through the activation of NF-κB, resulting in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL6, TNF.
source: Meanwhile, the pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling pathway primarily operates through the activation of NF-κB, resulting in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL6, TNF, etc. (Fitzgerald et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ORMDL3 is located at the core of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex, where it stabilizes SPT assembly.
source: ORMDL3 is a multiple transmembrane structural protein located at the core of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex, where it stabilizes SPT assembly (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature.

claim: ORMDL3 has been implicated in calcium transport.
source: ORMDL3 has also been implicated in calcium transport (Carreras-Sureda et al., 2013; Cantero-Recasens et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing literature.

claim: USP10 is indispensable for ORMDL3-mediated RIG-I degradation.
source: Furthermore, we discovered that the deubiquitinating enzyme USP10 stabilizes RIG-I, while ORMDL3 disturbs this process, thereby negatively regulating type I IFN production. When USP10 was knocked down, ORMDL3 was unable to degrade RIG-I-N, indicating that USP10 is indispensable for ORMDL3-mediated RIG-I degradation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ORMDL3 cannot degrade RIG-I when USP10 is knocked down.

claim: ORMDL3 forms a complex with MAVS and promotes the degradation of RIG-I, thereby attenuating the transcription of type I IFN and cytotoxic CD8+ T cell-mediated tumor killing.
source: Collectively, our findings identify ORMDL3 as a negative regulator of type I IFN pathway and anti-tumor immunity. The proposed working model is that ORMDL3 forms a complex with MAVS and promotes the degradation of RIG-I, thereby attenuating the transcription of type I IFN and cytotoxic CD8+ T cell-mediated tumor killing (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the working model based on all experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: This negative regulatory loop of antiviral innate immunity mediated by ORMDL3 may provide insights for the development of therapeutics against viral infections and tumors.
source: This negative regulatory loop of antiviral innate immunity mediated by ORMDL3 may provide insights for the development of therapeutics against viral infections and tumors.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.
